The point has been brought up by many hon. members that veterans receiving pensions under section 21 are not likely to benefit under this bill. As has been pointed out, however, the pension paid under this section of the act is one which is determined by the pension commission. It is not paid as of right, but the rate on which it is based may be the same as that of the disability pensioner who receives a pension under the act as a matter of entitlement. The last time increases were introduced in the Pension Act every pension paid, under section 21 for what is called meritorious service, either to the veteran himself or to the widow, was re-examined by the commission. I believe the assurance which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) referred to as having been given in the committee at that time was that every one of these cases would be reviewed in the light of the new increases, and I am certainly happy to tell the house that this procedure will be followed again this time.
The same procedure will apply to pensions paid to dependent parents. There again these pensions are paid after a full investigation by the commission. I do not think it is necessary for me to give all the details of the procedure followed, but briefly when an application for payment is received the commission arranges for a pension visitor to call on the applicant. He submits a report containing full information as to the physical condition and economic circumstances of the applicant. Where there are unmarried children living with the parents who, in the opinion of the commission, should be earning sufficient to permit them to contribute to the support of such parent, section 33 (6) of the

Pension Act
act provides that such child shall be deemed to be contributing not less than $10 per month for such support. This is the procedure that has been followed, and the cases of dependent parents will also be reviewed by the commission in the light of the increases that have been given. That of course will be done within the statutory limits. I might point out to hon. members, however, that while I do not know the exact number, I am informed that only a very small percentage at this time receive the full amount under the statute. This comes about as the result of investigations carried on by the commission. It might also be taken into account that of the slightly more than 11,000 dependent parents-that is, those who are receiving single pensions as fathers or as mothers, or where both parents are receiving them-over 5,000 will be qualifying under the old age security legislation after the first of January.
A further point has been mentioned by a number of members during the debate, when they have suggested that a section should be introduced into the bill so that increases made effective by this measure will not be considered as income for the purpose of war veterans allowances. The example was given of the procedure followed in 1948, when the last increases were brought forward. The bill introduced at that time stated that an increase in pension paid to any person by virtue of the section, in respect of any period prior to the day on which the act was to receive royal assent, was not to be included as income for the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946. The circumstances existing at that time which made necessary the introduction of that section were not the same as those existing today. It will be recalled that at that time the increases were voted by parliament after having been considered in the spring of the year-perhaps it was in June-by the parliamentary committee. It had been announced that these increases in the rates would be retroactive to October 1, 1947. So in order that the recipients of war veterans allowances who had received payments between October 1 and the date when the new increases became effective would not be considered as having received overpayment under the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act, and as a result have their payments reduced for a period of months, this section was introduced.
I am sure if hon. members who discussed the point this afternoon will refer to the report of the parliamentary committee of 1948, at which time the amendment was introduced-and while I may be mistaken I
believe it was brought forward at the suggestion of the then chairman, who is now my parliamentary assistant-they will see that amendment was put in the act after it had been pointed out that, without it, the effect of the act would be to bring about overpayment to recipients of war veterans allowances. As I said before, under this measure the increases are to come into force on January 1. Whatever changes may be decided upon by the committee at the next session will be made retroactive to the first of January. So the situation which existed in 1948, and which made that section necessary, does not exist today.
I believe that is all I had intended to say at this time, with the exception of possibly adding a few words along the lines followed by other hon. members during the course of the debate, both on the resolution and on the bill.
Hon. members have said that the meritorious features of the legislation can be traced to the work of the veterans organizations in Canada. I would be the last to make any effort to deny the efficiency of the work done by those organizations, by the Canadian Legion on the one hand and the national council of veterans associations on the other. As Minister of Veterans Affairs it is my good fortune to administer a department which has to deal with a large section of the Canadian population. In so doing I have always been able to count on the co-operation and advice of the main bodies comprising this section of the veteran population. It is a relationship I have always appreciated, and one I hope will continue. Much has been said in the house on previous occasions with respect to legislation affecting veterans, legislation which has resulted from what I might describe as round-table conferences between these veteran groups and the department. I pay them this tribute today, and express the hope that this happy relationship may continue.

They will get a bit of an increase, but their means will be assessed in the light of the new $40 and they will end up not with the $40 old age security as a net increase over their present position; and as a result of this review it is likely that there will be some cases that will not end up with any increase at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: They will end up with an over-all increase in income.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
They may end up with an amount that will give them an over-all increase in income but it is not likely that it will be an increase to the extent of the full $40 which will be the case with so many of our older Canadians, again because there is a means test in section 33 of this act as there is-I know you are looking at me with a frown, Mr. Chairman, and I will just say this one word and then leave this subject- in the War Veterans Allowance Act as well.
To get back in order, Mr. Chairman, or in other words to get back to this specific act, may I say that the discussion we have had underlines more clearly than before the need for increasing the ceiling in column 2 of schedule B and for permitting payment of pensions to dependent parents equal to the increased amount that will be allowed to widows of veterans. The widow's pension is being brought up to $100 a month, and properly so; the whole house is grateful for that. I think the same amount should be the figure for dependent parents.
From the minister's statement it would appear that the main reason for making this change is that several thousand of the dependent parents are over 70 years of age.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No.
And that they will be receiving the old age pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I never said that.

The minister has mentioned two or three times that 5,000 or more were

now to get the old age pension. But surely that is not sufficient reason for changing this schedule. Previously the figure was set at S900 for the widows and for the dependent parents. The figure is raised to $1,200 for the widow but remains at $900 for the dependent parents. It does seem to me that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is right when he pleads for an increase to $1,200 in the ceiling on the pension that can be paid to the dependent parents. I do not think the minister has advanced sufficient reasons for failing to increase that figure in this particular case.

On section 2-Coming into force.

Before we discuss clause 2 I should like to move an amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre, reading as follows:
That the following section be added as section 1 (a) of Bill No. 27:
1. (a) An increase in pension paid to any person by virtue of section 1 shall not be included as income for the purposes of the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I will put the amendment before the committee.

As I pointed out in my remarks on second reading, this is similar wording to that which was used in the amendment to the Pension Act contained in chapter 23 of the statutes of 1948. Here we have this position. The Department of Veterans Affairs administers both the pension and the war veterans allowance. A bill is brought in to increase the pension, and in the case of the small pensioner the result is to cut the war veterans allowance so that in a good many thousand cases these pensioners will get no benefit whatever from the increase now being brought in unless there is some provision that they will not have the same or some amount deducted from the war veterans allowance.
I do not intend to repeat the submission I made earlier in the afternoon, but I do urge upon the minister that he accept this amendment. If he does, the result will be that when the pension increases come into effect on January 1, 1952, the small pensioners who are drawing war veterans allowance will be able to get this increase without taking a cut in the war veterans allowance which, of course, would result in their income being just the same as it is today.
The minister has referred to the amendment to the Pension Act which was passed in 1948, and has pointed out, just as I did in my remarks, that the provision in that act
Pension Act
referred to a lump sum payment which was going to pensioners because the increase in pension was made retroactive for a period of approximately six months. He said because there was that difference there was no reason to make any such amendment to the present act. Actually, if he administers -the War Veterans Allowance Act properly during these winter months he will have exactly the same situation, because the increase in pension will constitute overpayments, and under the law his war veterans allowance board will have to take those overpayments into consideration. In that way the amount received by the pensioner will be cut back to what he would have received if there had been no increase.
The main consideration here should be to make certain that these small pensioners, who are also on war veterans allowance, get the benefit of this pension increase. It will not be very great for them because they are not the pensioners receiving high amounts. I think the maximum would be a 35 per cent single pensioner and a 45 per cent pensioner if married, because over and above those figures the pensioner cannot qualify for any war veterans allowance. Therefore the increase in pension will not run into very large amounts; but for these veterans every five cents means a great deal. Every five cents or ten cents may mean the difference between getting a meal or not getting it. With prices high, as they are, and going higher all the time, many of these men are suffering greatly and will suffer more during the winter weather. I would urge on the minister that he accept this amendment. If it is not exactly in the proper terms, then accept an amendment which would bring about the result I am after, which is that the increase in pension given with the right hand shall not be taken away with the left because the war veterans allowance is reduced.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must say that I have very great doubt about the amendment being in order, because it has the effect of increasing the charge on the public exchequer and such an amendment must be moved by a minister of the crown. I will be glad to hear hon. members on the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think you should have no doubt about it. Even the hon. member arguing his amendment pleaded with the minister to accept it, even though it did not meet all the conditions, and make it his own amendment, or put it in other terms.

That shows how generous he is.

Pension Act

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He did it in a very able way, and I congratulate him. But in his own mind he knows that this will increase the expenditure which was announced in the message the minister gave when he first brought in the resolution. The hon. member made quite a plea for the committee to agree to the amendment, but if he looks at section 54 of the British North America Act he will see that a member, and even a minister, cannot move an amendment to increase an outlay without communicating to the house a message from the governor general. This would certainly increase the amount. There would be no object in moving the amendment if it did not increase the amount to be spent on the veterans. I really think that the hon. member will admit that his amendment is out of order.

The Minister of Public Works is perfectly right when he says it would mean a larger payment to these small pensioners. I would hope that the minister himself would agree to some such provision being written into the law so these men will not suffer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think even the minister could move that amendment at this stage. We would have to refer the matter back and submit it to the governor general, and then give the message to the house that he has been informed of the subject matter of the resolution and recommends it to the consideration of the house. We would not be in order in moving it at this stage in committee.

I am sure that would be a very easy thing to do. I suggest the minister do that immediately in order to meet a situation with which apparently the minister agrees but which, as he says, is faced with difficulties.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I never agreed that this should be done.

speechtext:
Citation 458 of Beauchesne's third edition reads:

May I just add my voice to that of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in urging the government to move the necessary resolution, get the permission of the governor general and so on. In other words, I urge the government to go through

the regular form and have something written into this bill so the situation which has been outlined will not continue, and those receiving small pensions may have them increased without the amount being taken off the war veterans allowance cheque if they are also recipients of that allowance. It seems ridiculous that a large number of pensioners who are drawing comparatively small disability pensions and are also in receipt of war veterans allowance should have the one cheque they receive increased, we will say by $10 or $15, and then have the war veterans allowance cheque knocked down by the same amount. Surely there are no insuperable difficulties in the way. It would not place any considerable strain on the treasury to do what has been suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and write something into this particular bill which would prevent that situation occurring.

I think we should be clear as to what will be the effect if the minister does not adopt this suggestion. Mr. Speaker, I suppose now that I can speak as a member of the bar of British Columbia it would be in order for me to say that I agree there is need for an increase in the number of judges which is provided by this bill. I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to ask the minister with regard to a matter about which I made inquiry the other day, namely the report in the press to the effect that under the prospective amendments to be suggested or which have already been suggested by the criminal law commission provision is being made for the extension of the jurisdiction of district or county court judges. Judges Act
commission. subtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF COUNTY COURT JUDGES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I confirm what I said on the last occasion when my learned friend inquired about this matter, that we have not as yet received a report, interim or otherwise, from the commission. subtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF COUNTY COURT JUDGES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a layman I want to say a few words about this bill. I suppose it might almost be considered presumption on my part to speak on a bill of this type, particularly following the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I know that an increase in the number of county court judges in the province of British Columbia is necessary because of the amount of work they have to do as a result of the increase in population. During the last two or three years I have noted that some of the county court judges are rather overworked. They are doing an immense amount of work at the present time, and that fact is not generally recognized by a large number of people.
In my opinion county court judges are a very important cog in the administration of justice. On the one hand there are the magistrates in the lower courts and on the other hand the justices of the higher courts, but it is my observation that the county court judges have the greatest amount to do with the greatest number of people. In years past I have had close association with some excellent county court judges in the interior of British Columbia, and it is generally recognized by people who know that they have rendered excellent service to the country.
During the war I had the opportunity of close association with some county court judges, particularly one who is now a justice of the supreme court of British Columbia, in connection with conciliation and arbitration boards. I shall never forget one case where one of these county court judges was the

Supreme Court Act
chairman of the board. Some of the workingmen interested in arbitration spoke to me. They were of the opinion that the judge would naturally be wholly in favour of one side and would support that side. As the hearings proceeded I was very interested to notice that, as the judge came in close contact with these men and as they listened to what he had to say, their opinion changed; and when the proceedings were over they willingly recognized his painstaking methods and fairness in approaching the question under dispute. I think the county court judges of British Columbia have performed excellent service in many fields that are strictly outside court work.
As far as my own district of Kootenay is concerned, we are very fortunate in having had a succession of excellent men acting as county court judges. I have been informed by a good number of people representing all parties in this house how much they appreciate the excellent work that is being done by the present incumbent of the office of county court judge in the Kootenays.

In connection with the bill
to which this resolution will lead, and in connection with the other bill the resolution leading to which is on the order paper, I might say that' these are cases where the ceiling of the emolument of the officer of the court is fixed by statute. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR

When was that statutory ceiling first provided?
[Mr. Herridge.l

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
I think it has always been in the statute in each case. If my hon. friend has not the statute before him, I have a pamphlet copy here if he wishes to see it. He will see that in setting up the office of registrar in each case it is provided that he shall exercise certain functions and shall be paid such salary as the governor general in council shall allow up to and not exceeding a certain sum. That is unlike other civil servants, who have no such statutory limit upon their salaries. The Department of Justice has received representations from the chief justice of Canada in the case of the supreme court, and from the president of the exchequer court in the case of that court, to the effect that it hardly seemed fair that these particular civil servants should be subject to such a ceiling which left their emoluments in a position of disparity as compared with those of other civil servants when the latter received increases in pay.
Our method of disposing of this request was to make a careful comparison with the emolument of the registrar of the supreme court of Ontario in Toronto, whose work is much the same in character, although in a court which would not ordinarily carry the same degree of dignity and importance as the Supreme Court of Canada. We have tried to relate the increase provided by the present amendment to the salary paid to the registrar of the Ontario high court at Osgoode hall.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: The minister stated that in arriving at the amount fixed in the bill for the salary of the registrar a comparison was made with the amount paid to the registrar of the Ontario high court of justice. Would the minister say what amount is paid to the official in question?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: What are the duties of a registrar, and what are his qualifications?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
I think perhaps I can answer that by giving you the qualifications of the gentlemen who hold these positions at the present time. In the case of the Exchequer Court of Canada, the gentleman in question is a barrister at law of forty years standing. After his appointment in 1908 as a Rhodes scholar from Manitoba he attended Oxford university, took the English bar examination there, and was called to the English bar in 1911. He was a member of the honourable society of the inner temple and later in the same year was admitted to the bar of

Manitoba. He practised law in Winnipeg from 1911 to 1923, later entering the dominion civil service where he acted for many years, until he was finally appointed to his present position. He is the chief administrative officer of the court. In addition to that he is a taxing officer, with authority to tax party and party costs which are incurred in court. Also, he has the jurisdiction of an exchequer court judge in chambers, and conducts inquiries into damages, in patent and other actions referred to him for that purpose.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: But the registrar has no judicial duties?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: He does not plead a case, decide a case or anything of that nature.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: As I have already indicated, his duties as a taxing officer are semi- or quasi-judicial, and his duties in exercising the jurisdiction of an exchequer court judge in chambers are judicial in character. Then his duties in connection with references to him under the act are also judicial in character. In that respect he compares to a master or referee in a high court.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: After all, he would be called only a clerk. A county court clerk would be the same thing.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: No, my hon. friend would be quite wrong in supposing that. The judicial duties of which I have spoken are altogether different from those of a county court clerk.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR

speakerposition: topic

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: What are the duties of this official? Does he not have the capacity of a clerk?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
No. Both these gentlemen to whom I have referred are registrars of courts. As I tried to explain a moment ago, the work of a registrar covers all the clerical duties my hon. friend has in mind in the case of the clerk of a county court; but in addition to that they have other duties of a quasi-judicial character, to which I have already made reference. For instance they have jurisdiction and power to try interlocutory motions of certain types which it would be quite proper to bring before a judge of the court. Lawyers who are involved in these cases come before the registrar to plead these interlocutory motions. The registrar, will sit on such motions and render a decision.
In the same way a judge of the court has power to refer certain matters back to the registrar for judicial decision. When these references are made the registrar of the court will sit and listen to counsel on both sides in precisely the same way a judge would, and will render judgment on the reference. So the registrar combines clerical duties with duties which I think might properly be described as judicial, or if not judicial in the exact sense, certainly they are quasi-judicial.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: They cannot plead a case.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: No. Any officer of the court has to be a barrister of several years standing, but once he is appointed he has to give up his practice of law. As a matter of fact, in connection with the court we are now discussing the position is very much a fulltime job, because the volume of business done by the Exchequer Court of Canada is very great.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
I am opposed to both these increases in salary, and for this reason: We have been struggling all along to get increases for people such as pensioners and persons on retirement incomes. Yet when we come to these higher positions, where the

Exchequer Court Act
salaries are already large and remunerative, the government goes to work and gives a big increase. Possibly it is all due to the surplus. These officials see an opportunity of getting something out of that immense surplus that may be on hand at the end of the year.
Notwithstanding what the Minister of Justice has just said, these men are just clerks, although they carry the glorified name of registrar. In our county courts throughout the provinces our clerks are doing the same class of work. Their qualifications may not be as high as those of registrars. I must say that I believe these increases are uncalled for under present conditions. These people cannot be described as overworked civil servants, or as civil servants overburdened with work. If you look at what a registrar or county court clerk does, you will find that he works about two hundred days a year. He is receiving a fine salary without any increase. If the minister wants to stand in properly with those for whom we have been pleading in the other branches of the service, and the men who have given war service, he should withdraw this measure. These men are overpaid now.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: In fairness to these gentlemen and the courts which they serve, I believe I should place on the record, in relation to the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Queens, the fact that in the supreme court of Ontario at Osgoode hall the senior master receives $8,500 a year, the master $7,500 and the registrar $7,500. When one takes into account the fact that the Exchequer Court of Canada receives business from one end of Canada to the other it does not seem unreasonable that the registrar of the exchequer court should get as much as but no more than the registrar of the supreme court of Ontario.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: When we were dealing with the supreme court amendment the minister was good enough to place on the record the qualifications of the registrar of the exchequer court. Since these two matters have become intertwined, perhaps he would be good enough to place on the record the qualifications of the registrar of the supreme court.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
I should be glad to do so. The gentleman who is now the registrar, Mr. Paul Leduc, was appointed as registrar of the supreme court on October 1, 1940. He had practised law in Ottawa from 1915 to 1934, at which time he became a cabinet minister in the Ontario government. He was a prominent member of the Belcourt firm of this city which did a great deal of agency work for firms in other parts of Canada, particularly

in the province of Quebec. In that way when he was appointed, although a lawyer residing in Ontario, he had had considerable experience in the Ontario practice and the civil law practice of the province of Quebec in relation to the appeals which would come to the supreme court from that province. He was a member of the bar of both provinces. I believe that in every respect he was qualified to become an official of the court.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Now that the supreme court, with the exception of the few appeals that are still en route or in the privy council, is the final court, what has the minister to say as to any increase in the duties and responsibilities of the registrar over what they were prior to the abolishment of appeals to the privy council?

speechtext: The hon. member is quite right in implying by his question that inevitably there will be an increase in the volume of work in the supreme court over what formerly obtained. As yet I do not think we have been able to accurately measure the extent of that increase.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Has the minister any statistics at all?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: No, we have not. One reason for not attempting to secure them is that we think the time is too short to accurately measure any increase in that work.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Has there been a material increase in consequence of making the supreme court the final court of appeal?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: I think I would be correct in saying there has been. I would not say a material increase, but a significant increase. Whether that is due to the abolition of appeals to the privy council I believe it would be difficult to say; for the time within which appeals from cases which were current at the time the amendment to the Supreme Court Act was passed has not yet run out. Until that time does run out the privy council is just as available as the court of last resort for cases then current as it has been heretofore. It will not be until that period has run out that we can trace with any accuracy the effect upon the volume of work in the supreme court which the abolition of appeals to the privy council might bring about.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: When will it run out?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: It is not a definite period. It will run out when the last time for appeal has lapsed for a case which was current in the trial court at the time the legislation came into effect. It is very difficult to forecast just when that will be.

I do not raise this by way of criticism at the moment, but I do believe something should be done to assure more expedition in the giving of judgments in the exchequer court. The delay in some of these cases is difficult to explain to one's clients. After all, in the administration of justice it is just as important that justice be rendered with expedition as it is that justice be rendered. I would suggest that the attention of the registrar be directed to the situation.
Has the minister any record before him showing the number of judgments that are a year and a half overdue, or even more than that? The situation is not due in any degree to the judges; nonetheless it is the subject of very strong criticism across the country.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR

A delay of one and a half or two years after a case has been heard might very well lead to a condition of affairs where the judge would remember the name of the case but the facts would long since have passed into the limbo of forgotten things. Regardless of the notes a judge takes, unless a judgment is delivered within a reasonable time certainly the client who loses the case is always of the opinion that had the judgment been given earlier the result might have been otherwise.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: I should like to ask one question about the registrar. At first, when the minister was speaking about him, I thought that he did all the work for the judges. But now I understand that he has a staff under him. What staff are under the registrar in carrying out his duties?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: I am afraid that I cannot at the moment give accurate figures in that regard. I shall be glad to get them and give them to my hon. friend. The registrar has a staff. He needs stenographers and clerical staff because the volume of litigation in these courts is large and a staff is required for that purpose. Then a good deal of the registrar's time is taken up with these judical duties that I was speaking about. The taxing of bills of costs takes up a great deal of time, as does the hearing of these interlocutory motions and the hearing of references. My hon. friend would be under a quite wrong impression if he thought that this gentleman was just a sort of glorified county court clerk with a staff of clerks under him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR

Both the hon. member for Queens and the Minister of Justice have addressed themselves to the question of

Exchequer Court Act
whether or not these registrars are persons of some importance or whether they are, in their words, just clerks. I think we should be careful about our use of that word. Sometimes a person who holds the position of clerk is an extremely important person.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: As to the actual number of cases handled, the volume would be substantially more in the Exchequer Court of Canada than in the Supreme Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Then does it follow that the work of the registrar of the exchequer court is heavier than that of the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: I did not say that. I said the work was greater in quantity but that the quality of responsibility involved was not necessarily as great. I think my hon. friend would probably agree that, having regard to the fact that one is a trial court and the other one is the highest court of appeal in the land, there is some ground for a distinction in salary between the two.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: But is it not true that in both cases the judicial functions exercised by these registrars are pretty much the same?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Well-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: I was rather interested in the answer the Minister of Justice gave to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He said that the work might be the same or a little more in quantity in the exchequer court but might differ in quality. I should like to know what he means by that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
What I said was the quality or the responsibility involved. The difference is this. To repeat myself, as I am bound to do because I think there is a certain

element of repetition in my hon. friend's question, may I say that the exchequer court, as my hon. friend knows, is the lowest trial court in respect of certain classes of action between the subject and the crown, patent actions and the like.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: That is, it is a court of first instance.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Yes, it is a court of first instance. If a case involves subject matter of that type it is tried before the exchequer court. The Supreme Court of Canada is the highest court of appeal in the whole country. It is the court of last resort. By statute the registrar is given the rank of a deputy minister. The representations we received were to the effect that we should have salaries higher than those which we have authorized, but these are the amounts that have been approved by treasury board. In arriving at them we have tried to make a comparison of the actual work done by these gentlemen -that is, the kind of the actual work done- with the work done by the registrars of other courts, particularly the supreme court of Ontario at Osgoode hall in Toronto.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Then am I to understand the situation is that as the supreme court is a higher court than the exchequer court- although both courts are dealing with the matter of justice-regardless of the amount of work done by the registrar of either court, in view of the fact that the registrar of the supreme court is connected with the highest court in the land as a matter of prestige his salary should be higher?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
I would not say that. If my hon. friend will reflect for a moment upon the fact that all the appeals from the ten provinces of Canada come to the Supreme Court of Canada, he will understand better what is involved. Not only appeals from the highest courts of these provinces but appeals from the county courts, if there are any, and also appeals from the Exchequer Court of Canada all come to the Supreme Court of Canada. In that way all of the more difficult and more controversial cases which have not, in the opinion of the counsel involved, been decided properly by the lower courts in the various provinces and in the exchequer court come to the Supreme Court of Canada. And the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada has a duty in relation to it corresponding to that of the registrars of these lower courts. If my hon. friend went to any one of the provinces he would find the same distinction between the county court clerk and the clerk of the higher court. No person argues that the county court clerk in large cities does not handle more

individual cases, but he does not get as large a salary because the quality of the responsibility which he has in relation to these cases is not considered to be as great as that of the registrar or clerk of the higher court, where usually larger amounts of money and more complicated legal issues are involved.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: Before the resolution carries I should like to get some idea of the number of cases this man would try. The minister says he has the power and the jurisdiction to try cases. Is there any way of forming some sort of estimate as to the average number of cases he would be called upon to try in the course of a year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
I should like to emphasize that this gentleman does not try any cases in the ordinary sense in which we usually use the word "case". What he tries are motions of what are called an interlocutory character; that is, for example, motions for an order for an examination for discovery, and other types of motions which are made before the actual trial of the case comes on and which would be made to the judge if the registrar did not have the authority to try them.
Another type of matter that the registrar tries is this. After the case is over he sits in judgment to determine what costs the successful party can tax against the unsuccessful party. In that connection he has to exercise the same type of judgment that a judge would exercise if he were determining the matter. Then he also has to deal with matters which are referred to him in his capacity as registrar by the judge, being matters of lesser importance than the trial of the case itself yet perhaps more detailed. He looks after those in a judicial capacity.
I must say that I cannot tell my hon. friend offhand how many these would be in number. I would have to get that information and supply it to him, but I have no doubt at all that they would be quite substantial. That is in addition to this other work of looking after all these documents and seeing that cases are properly set down, subpoenas are issued and all the other work a registrar does.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext: I must confess that all this is entirely new to me, but that does not make any difference to my responsibility as being one of those in this house who should contribute a little bit toward looking after the public purse. I shall have to ask a question or two to become informed on the matter. I should like to get some sort of idea of how much time on the average would be involved in trying one of these interlocutory cases.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
Oh, oh.
Exchequer Court Act

speechtext: To the lawyers it is clear; it is a matter for fun. Well, it would not be a matter of fun to some of the farmers who have a mortgage on their property. I do not mind paying this man; I have no objection at all to that, but I do feel that before we vote unanimously on a proposal like this we should get some sort of satisfaction as to whether or not the man is really earning the money.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM SALARY OF REGISTRAR
speechtext:
I do not know how I can emphasize any more strongly than I have already attempted to do that these positions are not in any sense sinecures. This particular position we are talking about, and in relation to which my hon. friend has just asked his question, is very much a full-time job that he works at the whole year round. In connection with that my hon. friend asks, how long does he spend on one of these interlocutory motions. I would say that it might range from perhaps an hour as a minimum to several hours. It depends upon the issues that are involved in the particular motion that comes before him. There will be a wide variation in the time it will take to deal with any one of these motions or references. It depends upon the facts and the points that are being raised and the like, and also probably upon the long-windedness of the counsel involved. Therefore no universally accurate answer can be given to my hon. friend's question. I do want to emphasize that this is not a matter of a man going down to the courthouse, hearing a motion and then going off to play golf or going home. He is there all the time in the ordinary course of his duties. When he absents himself from his office to hear these motions that are made [DOT]before him, or to deal with these references, the office has to remain open for the filing of papers, the issuing of court documents and the like, and that is the reason he has to have a staff.

Mr. Speaker, this has a little more to it than met the eye when one looked at the resolution. I have referred to the salaries of the civil service commissioners several times as an example of something that needs to be tidied up in our financial administration. The Secretary of State has just pointed out their salaries are fixed by statute at a certain amount, but in addition to that they have been receiving a further $2,000 by virtue of items in the estimates. For example, in the estimates of the current year, passed in the session that ended last June, there is item 76 which includes $2,000 for each of the commissioners additional to the amount provided by chapter 53 of the statutes of 1947. I have pointed out several times how the Auditor General has frowned upon this practice. He has stated that we should not legislate by having an item in the estimates year after year. If there is something we want to make permanent it should be written into the statutes. I have suggested several times that that recommendation of the Auditor General should be implemented, namely that this statute should be amended so as to provide therein for the full amount of salary being paid to the civil service commissioners.
When I saw this resolution on the order paper I complimented the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley), when I was speaking on the Financial Administration Act, upon what I felt was the intent of this resolution. From what has just been said I gather that this resolution goes a great deal further. It will take the question of the salaries of the civil service commissioners right out of the statute, right out of the control of parliament, and make them subject only to the governor in council. I strongly object to that being done.
We have just had a debate on two measures which fixed salaries by statute. There was no change in the general principle of parliamentary control over those salaries. Earlier we

passed an amendment to the Judges Act in which the salaries of judges are fixed by statute. The salaries of cabinet minister are fixed by statute. I realize that the salaries of deputy ministers are not, and in fact I was surprised the other night when 1 learned that the salary of a certain deputy minister had been increased over and above what was indicated in the current estimates.
I think we should have some explanation as to why we are being asked to change the statute in this way. I think the government should tell us also whether they have any intention after this bill is passed of increasing the salaries of the civil service commissioners. At the present time they receive by way of statute and an item in the estimates $12,000 for the chief commissioner and $10,000 for the other two. I was sympathetic with the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) a while ago in his attitude toward raising these other salaries, but those were salaries in brackets lower than these now under review.
As I say, I am wondering whether the bill to be based on this resolution will increase these salaries. At least we in parliament know in most cases what is happening, whereas this proposal seems to take this matter right out of our control. I question whether we should be asked to accept this without further explanation, without the government taking parliament completely into their confidence as to their plans.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING TENURE OF OFFICE AND SALARIES OF COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I wish to protest at having a resolution in these terms placed before us. There is nothing in this resolution to indicate what the legislation to follow is to be. If we are not told that in the resolution, we may as well have no resolution at all. How are hon. members going to be able to prepare themselves to debate the substance of legislation if there is nothing in a resolution to indicate what is going to be done? To use the vulgar term, in the sense that it is common, a resolution like this is merely making monkeys out of hon. members. The Civil Service Act is to be amended in a very important way and there is no indication whatsoever in the resolution as to what is to be done. Surely the house is entitled to more respect. What was referred to the governor general? What was he told? The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Civil Service Act in respect of the tenure of office and salaries of the commissioners.
I know what I would say if I were the governor general. I do not think I would

take it under consideration when I was offered a resolution like that. I would tell the fellow to bring me back a resolution that meant something, that I could understand. There is nothing in this resolution that indicates anything. The government may be going to abolish the Civil Service Act altogether. They may be going to pay the civil service commissioners $100,000 a year instead of $10,000 or $12,000, or they may be going to reduce them to $1,000. It is just the sheerest nonsense, and I am surprised that the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) should offer so little explanation when asked to explain the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, there are a few minutes left before adjournment, and I want to protest most strongly against defamation of the language of the law by some translators. They are crazy, and I say that with reference to the translators of legislation that comes before the House of Commons. Some members protested before the committee and some members are indifferent. The minister knows about the situation. Why is it that some translators, whom I will describe in French as "abrutis, moches et mabouls"- there can be no stronger expression-try to discover words that are understood by no one? Do they suffer from neurasthenia? What kind of disease have they in their brains? They are awful. This kind of legislation has to be applied by many people throughout the country who do not speak English, and!

On Monday we will continue and hope to conclude the debate on the address. Then we will take up third
reading of Bill No. 34, an act to amend the Public Printing and Stationery Act. Then we will proceed with Bill No. 30, an act to amend the Supreme Court Act; Bill No. 31, an act to amend the Exchequer Court Act. Then we will take up the resolution in the name of the Secretary of State to amend the Civil Service Act and the other resolution in the name of the same minister to amend the Dominion Elections Act.
At 6.15 p.m. the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to the order of the house passed on November 2, 1951.
